name: Palula
confidence_why: Liljegren's 2016 reference grammar, backed by Liljegren and Haider's 2009 IPA illustration, describes a contrastive, lexically placed mora-based pitch accent with minimal pairs, and the only dissent is Morgenstierne's brief 1941 field notes, which describe quantity-driven stress and report noticing no tone but are hedged and rest on far less material than the later long-term fieldwork.

new_statements.quote: "Main stress falls on the final or the penultimate syllable of the lexical root. One of the vocalic moras of the stressed syllable receives pitch accent [...] Pitch accent is contrastive" (p. 44). "[T]he location of the accent within a given word is not entirely predictable. Therefore, accent in Palula must be defined as lexical." (p. 73). "Accent falls either on the final or the penultimate syllable in a non-verbal lexical stem [...]; whereas in verbal stems [...] the accent is always on the final syllable. In terms of vocalic moras, only one of the three last moras, of any lexical stem in Palula, may be the locus of the pitch accent." (p. 74)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Each phonological word (bare stem or stem plus suffixes) carries exactly one accent, realised as higher pitch (with some extra amplitude) on a single vocalic mora: a short vowel, or the first (falling) or second (rising) mora of a long vowel. Its position is lexical within limits: on non-verbal stems it sits on the final or the penultimate syllable (one of the last three moras), on verbal stems always on the final syllable. Accent-bearing suffixes (plural -í, oblique -í, present -áan, infinitive -áai, etc.) remove the stem accent and take it themselves; accent-neutral suffixes normally leave the stem accent in place. Minimal pairs by accent position/mora exist (káti 'saddle' vs katí 'how many?', čúur 'four' vs čuúr 'hot fire').
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; the grammar states a word 'may carry one, and only one, accent' (p. 72). The word 'stress' beyond the p. 44 summary is used only for a compound's 'primary stressed part' (p. 71) and for historical OIA accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Under certain conditions the stem accent shifts onto an accent-neutral suffix (§3.5.1, pp. 75ff., with segmental alternations, e.g. ṣiṣ~ṣiṣóom); a small class of 'accent-shifting T-verbs' (§9.3.7, p. 216); some suffix allomorphy (-áan/-éen/-áand). Morgenstierne 1941 (§9, p. 11) described stress impressionistically as falling on the first long syllable from the end, no further back than the antepenult, with no tone noticed; Liljegren's mora-accent analysis supersedes this.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (stem or stem+suffixes); the p. 44 statement refers to the lexical root, the p. 74 statement to lexical stems; suffix behaviour is stated separately. Postpositions 'tend to receive stress like other free morphemes' (p. 143). Description covers both main dialects, Ashret (A) and Biori (B), with A as primary.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog phal1254 Palula = Phalura/Phalūṛa (Morgenstierne 1941) = Dangarikwar/Ashreti; Liljegren 2016 covers both main dialects, Ashret (A, primary) and Biori (B), and states the accent facts for both. The related Sawi sketch (Bashir 2003, pp. 887-889) concerns a distinct language in Afghanistan, not this key.

new_statements.relation_note: already held by the project from the 2026-09-17 pass, re-read here. Differs in TYPE from the catalog's existing statement (Liljegren 2016: lexically defined mora pitch accent, not predictable): Morgenstierne describes a quantity-driven stress rule and explicitly denies any tone. The two are compatible on the window (Morgenstierne: not further back than the antepenult; Liljegren: one of the last three moras of the stem), but not on predictability. Morgenstierne's 1941 notes rest on a brief visit; Liljegren's account rests on long fieldwork and is the one to prefer.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress on the rightmost long (heavy) syllable, limited to a three-syllable window at the right edge (never further left than the antepenult); in some words a long penult takes the stress even when the final is also long. No lexical or morphological tone noticed.
new_statements.exceptions: Some words stress a long penult even when the final syllable is long (examples given, scanned too noisy to transcribe reliably).
new_statements.identity_note: Liljegren 2016 describes both the Ashret and Biori dialects of Palula (Chitral); Liljegren & Haider 2009 is based on the Ashret variety (speaker Naseem Haider). Morgenstierne 1941 uses 'A(shreti)' and numbered informant/dialect sigla in the noisy scan; the stress statement is given for the language generally.

Phonetically the accent is primarily realized as relatively higher pitch, accompanied to some extent by higher amplitude. [...] The accent-bearing unit is the mora. [...] Even though some combinations of syllables and accents are more common than others, and there are restrictions on accent placement, the location of the accent within a given word is not entirely predictable. In some cases, difference in accent placement is the only phonemic contrast between two lexical items: séeti 'thigh' vs. seetí 'having looked after'

new_statements.rule_in_words: One culminative pitch accent per phonological word, borne by a vocalic mora (short vowel, or first or second mora of a long vowel); placement is restricted but not predictable, so it is lexical; minimal pairs exist.
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the general statement that placement is lexical.

new_statements.relation_note: already held by the project and the source of the catalog's existing statement, re-read here to verify pp. 44, 73, 74. Confirms the existing quote and adds the stem-position rule (non-verbal final/penult, verbal final, three-mora window) and the accent-bearing vs accent-neutral suffix classes. Covers both the Ashret and Biori dialects.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lexical mora-based pitch accent, one per word (p. 44: 'Main stress falls on the final or the penultimate syllable of the lexical root'; p. 73: 'the location of the accent within a given word is not entirely predictable. Therefore, accent in Palula must be defined as lexical'). Within the stem the accent sits on one of the last three moras: non-verbal stems final or penult syllable, verbal stems always final. Accent-bearing suffixes take the word accent away from the stem; accent-neutral suffixes usually leave it, with some conditioned shifts (§3.5.1).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; explicitly one and only one accent per phonological word.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent shifts from stem to accent-neutral suffix under certain conditions (§3.5.1); accent-shifting verbs (§9.3.7, p. 216); minimal pairs by accent placement (p. 74: čúur 'four' vs čuúr 'hot fire', káti 'saddle' vs katí 'how many?').
new_statements.identity_note: Liljegren 2016 describes both the Ashret and Biori dialects of Palula (Chitral); Liljegren & Haider 2009 is based on the Ashret variety (speaker Naseem Haider). Morgenstierne 1941 uses 'A(shreti)' and numbered informant/dialect sigla in the noisy scan; the stress statement is given for the language generally.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement, between eras rather than within one: Morgenstierne 1941 (§9, p. 11) treats Palula as having quantity-sensitive stress (rightmost long syllable, not further back than the antepenult, with some long penults winning over long finals) and states he noticed no lexical or morphological tone, whereas Liljegren (& Haider 2009 p. 385; 2016 pp. 44, 73-74) analyses a lexically defined, culminative, mora-based pitch accent that is not predictable and yields minimal pairs. The two agree on the right-edge window (antepenult limit / last three moras) but differ on type and predictability; Liljegren's account, based on long-term fieldwork and instrumental phonetics, supersedes the 1941 notes. The only listed work (Liljegren 2008 thesis) could not be opened, so it neither confirms nor challenges this.
